prompt: An App Runner service on the default settings gets no visitors for a whole month. What is it billed for?
hint: Two meters, and one of them runs whether anybody visits or not.

choices.text: Nothing, because App Runner scales a quiet service down to zero instances
choices.why: MinSize cannot go below one. Only PauseService takes capacity to zero, and somebody has to call it.

choices.text: The memory of one provisioned instance
choices.why: Right. Memory is billed for every provisioned instance; the processor only while one serves. 2 GB × 0.007 × 730 is 10.22 USD.

choices.text: The processor and the memory of one instance, all month
choices.why: That is the bill of an instance that is active all month, 56.94 USD. An idle one pays memory alone.

choices.text: The memory of the 25 instances that MaxSize allows
choices.why: MaxSize is a ceiling for busy times. A quiet service keeps MinSize instances, which is one.

prompt: An App Runner service with one instance of 1 vCPU and 2 GB is active for 300 hours of a 730-hour month and idle for the rest. At 0.064 USD per vCPU-hour and 0.007 USD per GB-hour, what is the month, in USD, to the cent?
hint: Active hours pay vCPU and memory, 0.078 an hour; idle hours pay memory only, 0.014 an hour.

prompt: You run aws apprunner list-services against moto and get a 500 with an HTML page in it. What does that tell you?
hint: Who wrote the page: AWS, or the program on your laptop?

choices.text: App Runner is not offered in us-east-1 either
choices.why: us-east-1 is where the price sheet reads App Runner from. And the answer did not come from AWS at all.

choices.text: moto does not implement App Runner
choices.why: Right. A 500 from moto is a service it has no code for; AWS would answer the command line in JSON, not with an HTML page.

choices.text: The credentials test and test were refused
choices.why: A refused credential is a named error such as InvalidClientTokenId, and moto accepts test anyway.

choices.text: AWS refused because the account is not an existing App Runner customer
choices.why: The request never reached AWS: AWS_ENDPOINT_URL sends it to moto on your laptop.

prompt: A company opens its first AWS account in October 2026 and wants exactly what App Runner offers: an image in, an address out. What does AWS's own documentation point it to?
hint: The service closed to new customers on a date in 2026, and its availability page names a successor.

choices.text: App Runner in us-east-1, since São Paulo does not offer it
choices.why: Changing region does not help. Since 30 April 2026 App Runner is closed to new customers in every region.

choices.text: Amazon ECS Express Mode
choices.why: Right. The availability-change page recommends it: one call that builds a Fargate service with its load balancer and scaling.

choices.text: A self-managed Kubernetes cluster on EC2, which is what App Runner ran on underneath
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation says that, and a cluster is the opposite of what the company asked for.

choices.text: App Runner through a VPC connector, which existing customers lend to new accounts
choices.why: A VPC connector lets a service reach a private network. It has nothing to do with who may sign up.

prompt: With the default auto scaling configuration, App Runner adds an instance once one instance has more than ___ requests in flight at the same time.
hint: The default of MaxConcurrency.

prompt: In Elastic Beanstalk, what is shop-prod when the application is called shop?
hint: Of the four words, which one has an address of its own?

choices.text: An application version: one zip of the code in S3
choices.why: A version is a build with a label such as v2. It runs nowhere until an environment deploys it.

choices.text: A platform
choices.why: A platform is the operating system, runtime and web server underneath, maintained by AWS.

choices.text: An environment: one running copy of one version
choices.why: Right. shop-prod and shop-staging are two environments of the same application.

choices.text: A second application, since every environment needs one of its own
choices.why: One application holds several environments. That is what the application is for.

prompt: moto answered create-environment. Which fields of its answer show that moto is imitating Beanstalk rather than running it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare each field with what AWS would have put there.

choices.text: EnvironmentId is an empty string
choices.why: AWS returns an id beginning with e-. moto left it empty.

choices.text: PlatformArn is TODO
choices.why: A note moto's authors left for themselves, where AWS names the platform.

choices.text: Status is Ready in the same second
choices.why: AWS answers Launching and builds for minutes. moto has nothing to build.

choices.text: ApplicationName is shop
choices.why: That is what the request named, and AWS would answer the same.

choices.text: Tier is WebServer
choices.why: A load-balanced web server is the tier a plain create-environment asks for on AWS too.

prompt: Put the steps of putting the shop on Elastic Beanstalk, on AWS, in order.
hint: The folder first, the running copy after the code exists.
items: create-application-version registers a zip in S3 as v2
create-environment starts a CloudFormation stack for shop-prod
The stack creates the group, the instances and the load balancer
trap: Creating the environment before a version exists gives it the sample application rather than yours.

prompt: A Beanstalk environment keeps three t4g.medium instances running all month. At 0.0536 USD an hour each and 730 hours, what do the instances cost, in USD, to the cent?
hint: Beanstalk itself adds nothing; count only the instances.

prompt: A colleague edits the listener of a Beanstalk environment's load balancer by hand, in the EC2 console, because no option seemed to reach it. What goes wrong later?
hint: Who believes they own that load balancer?

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong, because Beanstalk reads the load balancer live each time and adopts the edit
choices.why: Beanstalk works through its stack, and the stack still describes the old listener.

choices.text: The environment is deleted as soon as Beanstalk notices a change made outside it
choices.why: Nothing is deleted. The trouble arrives later, quietly.

choices.text: A later Beanstalk change reverts the edit, or fails against a stack that no longer matches
choices.why: Right. The resources are ordinary, but the stack that made them still thinks it owns them.

choices.text: The console refuses the edit, because resources a Beanstalk stack created are locked against changes
choices.why: They are ordinary resources and the console lets you change them, which is the danger.

prompt: Match each Beanstalk deployment policy to what happens while it deploys.
hint: Ask of each one: does capacity drop, and what is left of the old version?

pairs.right: Every instance at once, and the site is down meanwhile
One batch at a time, with capacity down by a batch
An extra batch first, so capacity holds
A full new set beside the old, swapped in when healthy
New instances take a share of requests for a set time

right_distractors: A second environment whose address is swapped

prompt: Which deployment policy leaves the old instances serving until the new ones are healthy, so that going back means terminating the new ones?
hint: Going back without deploying the old version again.

choices.text: Rolling
choices.why: Rolling replaces instances batch by batch. Going back is deploying the old version again.

choices.text: RollingWithAdditionalBatch
choices.why: The extra batch keeps capacity up, but the old instances are still updated in place, and going back is another deployment.

choices.text: Immutable
choices.why: Right. The new set runs beside the old; if it fails its health checks, it is terminated and the old set never changed.

choices.text: AllAtOnce, since it is the fastest to undo
choices.why: It is the fastest to run, with the site down. Undoing it is a second deployment just as fast and just as down.

prompt: An environment with MinSize 3 on t4g.medium (0.0536 USD an hour) deploys with the Immutable policy. While old and new sets run together, what do the instances cost per hour, in USD?
hint: An immutable deployment runs a complete second set beside the first.

prompt: shop.config sets PreferredStartTime to "Sun:05:00" for managed platform updates. When does the window start for a team in São Paulo, three hours behind UTC?
hint: The time in that option is UTC.

choices.text: Sunday at 05:00
choices.why: That is the time in UTC. São Paulo is three hours behind it.

choices.text: Sunday at 02:00
choices.why: Right. 05:00 UTC less three hours is 02:00 in São Paulo, a quiet hour for a shop.

choices.text: Sunday at 08:00
choices.why: That adds the three hours instead of taking them away.

choices.text: Saturday at 21:00
choices.why: That takes away eight hours, which is no time zone the shop is in.

prompt: Beanstalk options that should travel with each version of the code are written in a file under the directory ___ inside the version's zip.
hint: A hidden directory whose name starts with a dot and the initials of the service.

prompt: Three developers, one Django shop, a new AWS account in October 2026, and now and then a need to log into a machine to look at a problem. Which of this lesson's options fits?
hint: Which one is open to them and still gives them a machine?

choices.text: App Runner, built from the Git repository
choices.why: It would fit the shape, but it is closed to new customers, and it gives no instance to log into.

choices.text: Elastic Beanstalk on the Python platform
choices.why: Right. It is open, it runs the app on EC2 instances in their account, and SSH is there when they need to look.

choices.text: An EKS cluster with managed node groups
choices.why: It works and it costs them a cluster to run and upgrade, which is the platform job they do not have anybody for.

choices.text: ECS Express Mode, for the SSH it adds to Fargate
choices.why: Express Mode builds a Fargate service, and Fargate gives no host to log into.

prompt: Which of these is a sign that a team has outgrown its platform service? Choose all that apply.
hint: The signal is the application stopping being ordinary, not the platform doing its job.

choices.text: A second and a third service now call each other privately, each with its own releases
choices.why: A platform built around one application starts to show its seams.

choices.text: A release must reach one customer's traffic first, as a canary
choices.why: That is more than the platform's deployment options offer.

choices.text: Traffic doubles from 10 to 20 requests a second
choices.why: Scaling is what the platform does for you. Growth alone is not a reason to leave.

choices.text: An agent has to run beside the application on every machine
choices.why: App Runner offers no way to; Beanstalk offers hooks that grow into a platform of their own.

choices.text: The platform applies a patch version in its weekly window
choices.why: That is managed updates working as configured.

prompt: A team still on App Runner wants the day it leaves to cost a week rather than a quarter. Which choice, made now, does most for that?
hint: What leaves with the application unchanged?

choices.text: Deploying from an image in ECR rather than from the source repository
choices.why: Right. The same image goes into a task definition of lesson 8; a source build leaves you to write the Dockerfile on the way out.

choices.text: Keeping the default awsapprunner.com address
choices.why: The address is the one thing every exit changes. A custom domain would help more than the default.

choices.text: Setting MinSize to 1
choices.why: That is the default, and it changes the bill, not the exit.

choices.text: Switching on automatic deployments
choices.why: It removes a pipeline from your side, which is one more thing to rebuild after leaving.

prompt: What does an Elastic Beanstalk worker environment do with the messages in its SQS queue?
hint: A worker has no load balancer in front of it.

choices.text: Its instances read them and post each one to your application over HTTP
choices.why: Right. The application receives a request per message, so a background job runs on the same platform as the site.

choices.text: It forwards them to Lambda, which runs your code for each
choices.why: No function is involved; the work runs on the environment's own instances.

choices.text: It stores them in S3 for the web environment to collect
choices.why: The queue already holds them. The worker's job is to deliver them to your code.

choices.text: It turns each message into a new application version and deploys it
choices.why: Versions are code. Messages are work for the code that is already deployed.

prompt: Where are the EC2 instances that serve a Beanstalk environment on AWS?
hint: App Runner hides the machines; Beanstalk does something else with them.

choices.text: In an account AWS owns, out of sight, as with App Runner
choices.why: That is App Runner's model. Beanstalk builds in yours.

choices.text: In your own account, created by the environment's CloudFormation stack
choices.why: Right. They are ordinary instances in an ordinary group, which you can list and must not edit by hand.

choices.text: Nowhere: Beanstalk is serverless, and it bills per request rather than by the hour
choices.why: Beanstalk bills nothing itself; the instances it builds are billed by the hour.

choices.text: In moto, which keeps them as records
choices.why: moto kept the environment as a record and built no instance at all: four empty lists.

prompt: Put the steps of an Immutable deployment in Beanstalk in order.
hint: The old instances are the last thing to change.
items: New instances with v2 are launched in a temporary group
The new instances pass their health checks
They are moved into the environment's own group
The instances running v1 are terminated
trap: Terminating the old instances before the new ones are healthy turns Immutable into AllAtOnce with extra steps.

prompt: During a deployment App Runner temporarily doubles a service's provisioned instances. What does that do to the bill?
hint: Which meter does a provisioned instance run?

choices.text: Nothing at all, because App Runner charges no fee for a deployment
choices.why: The deployment itself carries no fee, but the extra copies are provisioned, and provisioned copies are billed.

choices.text: Memory charges for the extra copies, until the switch is over
choices.why: Right. Memory is billed for every provisioned instance; the processor only for the ones that serve.

choices.text: A full month of a second instance, since one was provisioned
choices.why: The doubling is temporary: it lasts the deployment, not the month.

choices.text: Twice the price per GB-hour, for as long as the deployment lasts
choices.why: The price stays 0.007. It is the number of instances that changes.

prompt: App Runner bills memory for every provisioned instance, and the processor only for the ___ ones.
hint: The ones serving requests at that moment.

prompt: What does Elastic Beanstalk itself charge for an environment?
hint: Separate the builder from what it builds.

choices.text: Nothing; you pay for what it creates
choices.why: Right. Two t4g.medium all month are 78.26 USD of instances, and Beanstalk adds nothing to that.

choices.text: A fee per environment per hour, on top of the instances
choices.why: There is no such fee. The bill is the resources.

choices.text: 0.064 USD per vCPU-hour, like App Runner
choices.why: That is App Runner's processor meter, in us-east-1.

choices.text: A fee per deployment, which is why AllAtOnce is cheapest
choices.why: Deployments carry no fee; AllAtOnce is the fastest, with the site down.
